title: DevOps & Cloud Mastery Quiz
description: Expert questions on Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, CI/CD, GitOps, monitoring, and cloud architecture.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
options: A. Image is a read-only layered template; container is a running instance of that image with a writable layer
B. Container is a read-only template; image is the running instance
C. They are the same thing stored in different locations
D. Image is stored in memory; container is stored on disk
questions.explain: An image is the static, read-only template built from a Dockerfile; a container adds a writable layer on top and is a live, running instance of that image.

questions.question: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, what does the '--target build' flag accomplish?
options: A. Names the final image 'build' in the local registry
B. Stops the build at the stage named 'build', skipping subsequent stages
C. Enables parallel execution of all stages up to 'build'
D. Copies only the 'build' stage artifacts to the host
questions.explain: --target lets you build only up to a named stage, which is useful for debugging an intermediate stage or producing a smaller image without the later stages.

questions.question: Which Docker run flag makes the container filesystem read-only, improving security posture?
options: A. --no-write
B. --immutable
C. --read-only
D. --ro-filesystem
questions.explain: --read-only mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only, preventing processes inside from writing to it and reducing the attack surface.

questions.question: In Kubernetes, what is the role of the 'etcd' component?
options: A. Schedules pods onto worker nodes based on resource availability
B. Routes traffic between pods using iptables rules
C. Manages container lifecycle on each worker node
D. Distributed key-value store — the single source of truth for all cluster state
questions.explain: etcd is the distributed, consistent key-value store that persists all cluster state, so every other control plane component reads from and writes to it.

questions.question: What does a Kubernetes Deployment's 'maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1' rolling update strategy guarantee?
options: A. One extra pod is created before any old pod is removed — capacity never drops below desired replicas
B. All pods are replaced simultaneously with zero downtime
C. Updates pause after each pod for manual approval
D. Only one pod runs at any time during the update
questions.explain: maxUnavailable: 0 forbids reducing capacity, so Kubernetes must surge one new pod up before terminating an old one, keeping full capacity throughout the rollout.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Kubernetes Service type 'ClusterIP' and 'LoadBalancer'?
options: A. ClusterIP exposes to internet; LoadBalancer is internal only
B. LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer; ClusterIP is only reachable within the cluster
C. ClusterIP is for TCP; LoadBalancer is for HTTP only
D. LoadBalancer auto-scales pods; ClusterIP does not
questions.explain: ClusterIP gives an internal-only virtual IP, while LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer that routes internet traffic to the service.

questions.question: What Kubernetes object ensures exactly one pod instance runs on every node in the cluster?
options: A. Deployment with replicas matching node count
B. StatefulSet
C. DaemonSet
D. ReplicaSet
questions.explain: A DaemonSet automatically schedules one copy of a pod onto every (or selected) node, which is ideal for node-level agents like log collectors or monitoring daemons.

questions.question: In Terraform, what is stored in the '.terraform.lock.hcl' file?
options: A. The encrypted state of all managed resources
B. Variable values for the current workspace
C. The plan output from the last 'terraform plan' run
D. Provider version constraints and checksums — ensures reproducible provider installations across team members
questions.explain: The lock file records exact provider versions and checksums so everyone on the team and in CI installs the identical, verified provider binaries.

questions.question: Which Terraform command imports an existing AWS S3 bucket into state management WITHOUT recreating it?
options: A. terraform import aws_s3_bucket.existing my-bucket-name
B. terraform apply -target=aws_s3_bucket.existing
C. terraform state add aws_s3_bucket.existing my-bucket-name
D. terraform refresh -resource=aws_s3_bucket.existing
questions.explain: terraform import binds an already-existing real-world resource to a resource address in state, letting Terraform manage it going forward without recreating it.

questions.question: What does 'terraform validate' check that 'terraform fmt' does not?
options: A. fmt checks syntax errors; validate only formats code
B. validate checks configuration correctness and internal consistency (valid references, required args); fmt only fixes code formatting
C. They check identical things — validate is just slower
D. validate compares state with cloud reality; fmt does not
questions.explain: terraform fmt only rewrites style and whitespace, while terraform validate checks that the configuration is internally consistent and syntactically correct.

questions.question: In GitOps with ArgoCD, what does 'self-heal: true' do?
options: A. Automatically fixes application bugs using AI analysis
B. Restarts crashed containers without human intervention
C. Reverts manual changes made directly to the cluster that drift from the Git-declared state
D. Heals broken Git merge conflicts automatically
questions.explain: Self-heal makes ArgoCD continuously reconcile live cluster state back to what is declared in Git, automatically undoing manual out-of-band changes.

questions.question: In GitHub Actions, which permission is required to request an OIDC token for keyless cloud authentication?
options: A. contents: write
B. packages: write
C. security-events: write
D. id-token: write
questions.explain: id-token: write allows the workflow to request a short-lived OIDC token from GitHub, which cloud providers trust instead of long-lived static credentials.

questions.question: What does pinning a GitHub Action by full SHA (e.g., uses: actions/checkout@abc1234...) protect against?
options: A. Supply chain attacks where a tag is moved to point to malicious code — SHA is immutable
B. Protects against the action becoming slow over time
C. Ensures the action only runs on Ubuntu runners
D. Prevents breaking changes from newer action versions
questions.explain: Tags like @v3 can be moved to point at different, potentially malicious code, but a commit SHA is immutable, guaranteeing you always run the exact reviewed code.

questions.question: What Prometheus function should you use on a counter metric to get requests per second?
options: A. increase()
B. rate()
C. delta()
D. avg_over_time()
questions.explain: rate() computes the per-second average rate of increase of a counter over a time window, which is exactly what is needed for requests-per-second.

questions.question: In the Google SRE Golden Signals framework, which signal is most directly tied to user experience?
options: A. Saturation — how full the service is
B. Traffic — how much demand exists
C. Latency — time to serve a request (the user waits for this)
D. Errors — rate of failed requests
questions.explain: Latency is the time a user directly experiences while waiting for a response, making it the signal most tightly coupled to perceived service quality.

questions.question: What is the primary security benefit of using Workload Identity (GKE) or IRSA (EKS) instead of environment variable credentials in pods?
options: A. Credentials are automatically rotated every 30 minutes instead of daily
B. Cloud provider encrypts the environment variables at rest
C. Access is audited by the Kubernetes API server rather than CloudTrail
D. No static long-lived credentials are stored anywhere — pods receive short-lived tokens via OIDC federation, reducing blast radius of credential theft
questions.explain: Workload Identity and IRSA eliminate stored static secrets by issuing short-lived tokens via OIDC federation, so a leaked token has limited lifetime and impact.

questions.question: What does 'immutable infrastructure' mean in practice?
options: A. Servers that cannot be modified after deployment — changes require replacing the server entirely with a new image, eliminating configuration drift
B. Infrastructure running on read-only filesystems
C. Infrastructure that is permanently hosted and never decommissioned
D. Containers that use read-only Docker images
questions.explain: Instead of patching servers in place, immutable infrastructure replaces them wholesale with a new image on every change, which prevents configuration drift.

questions.question: In Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, what happens by default if no NetworkPolicy selects a pod?
options: A. All ingress and egress traffic to/from the pod is blocked
B. All ingress and egress traffic to/from the pod is allowed
C. Ingress is blocked; egress is allowed by default
D. The pod is automatically placed in a quarantine namespace
questions.explain: Kubernetes networking is unrestricted by default, so a pod not selected by any NetworkPolicy can send and receive traffic freely until a policy restricts it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)?
options: A. Limits CPU and memory spending per pod
B. Controls pod scheduling priority relative to other pods
C. Ensures a minimum number of pods remain available during voluntary disruptions like node drains or rolling updates
D. Sets cost budgets for cloud resources consumed by pods
questions.explain: A PDB tells the cluster how many pods of an app must stay running during voluntary disruptions such as node drains, preventing accidental over-eviction.

questions.question: Which Helm command upgrades a release but rolls back automatically if the deployment fails?
options: A. helm upgrade --force myrelease ./chart
B. helm upgrade --wait --timeout 300s myrelease ./chart
C. helm rollout upgrade myrelease ./chart
D. helm upgrade --atomic myrelease ./chart
questions.explain: The --atomic flag makes Helm wait for the upgrade to succeed and automatically roll back to the previous release if it fails, keeping the release in a working state.

questions.question: What AWS component allows private access to S3 from within a VPC without traffic traversing the internet?
options: A. VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3
B. NAT Gateway
C. Transit Gateway
D. PrivateLink Interface Endpoint
questions.explain: A VPC Gateway Endpoint routes S3 traffic privately within AWS's network via route table entries, avoiding the public internet and NAT gateway costs entirely.

questions.question: In a CI/CD pipeline, what is a 'canary deployment' and what metric triggers rollback?
options: A. Deploy to a test environment only; rollback if tests fail
B. Route a small percentage of traffic to the new version; monitor error rate and latency — if SLO thresholds are breached, roll back automatically
C. Deploy to one availability zone first; rollback if health checks fail
D. A blue/green deployment with a canary test user group
questions.explain: A canary deployment exposes the new version to a small slice of real traffic while monitoring error rate and latency, rolling back automatically if SLOs are breached.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) in DevSecOps?
options: A. A billing document for cloud resource usage
B. A manifest file listing all Kubernetes resources in a namespace
C. A complete inventory of all software components, libraries, and their versions in an artifact — enables rapid CVE impact assessment
D. A bill of Terraform resources to be provisioned
questions.explain: An SBOM lists every component and version bundled into a software artifact, so when a new CVE is disclosed, teams can instantly see which systems are affected.

questions.question: In Kubernetes, what does 'kubectl rollout undo deployment/api' roll back to?
options: A. The initial deployment when the Deployment was first created
B. A specific revision number must be provided — the command alone fails
C. Clears all rollout history and resets to the chart default
D. The previous revision — the last known-good ReplicaSet before the current one
questions.explain: Without a --to-revision flag, rollout undo reverts the Deployment to the immediately preceding ReplicaSet revision, effectively undoing the last rollout.

questions.question: What does the Ansible 'handlers' section in a playbook do?
options: A. Defines tasks triggered by 'notify' — run once at the end of a play only if notified, useful for restarting services only when config changes
B. Defines tasks that always run, regardless of whether changes occurred
C. Handles errors and provides fallback tasks for failures
D. Manages inventory host groups and connection handlers
questions.explain: Handlers only run when explicitly notified by a task that reported a change, and they run once at the end of the play, which is ideal for conditional service restarts.

questions.question: In GCP's resource hierarchy, what is the correct order from top to bottom?
options: A. Organization → Folders → Projects → Resources
B. Projects → Organization → Folders → Resources
C. Resources → Projects → Folders → Organization
D. Folders → Organization → Projects → Resources
questions.explain: GCP's hierarchy flows Organization (root) → Folders (optional grouping) → Projects → Resources, with IAM policies inherited downward.

questions.question: Which GCP compute option is best for stateless HTTP containers that scale to zero when idle?
options: A. Compute Engine
B. Cloud Run
C. GKE Autopilot
D. Bare Metal Solution
questions.explain: Cloud Run runs stateless containers triggered by HTTP/events and bills per 100ms of CPU/memory, scaling to zero when there's no traffic.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a GCP Service Account?
options: A. A human user's login identity for the Cloud Console
B. A special identity used by applications/VMs to authenticate to GCP APIs
C. A billing account shared across projects
D. A support ticket queue for GCP Premium Support
questions.explain: Service accounts are non-human identities that workloads use to call GCP APIs, avoiding embedded user credentials.

questions.question: In GCP IAM, what is the recommended best practice for assigning permissions?
options: A. Always grant the Owner role to simplify management
B. Prefer predefined roles over basic roles, and grant least privilege
C. Share one service account key across all environments
D. Grant Editor role to every service account by default
questions.explain: Predefined roles scope permissions to specific services (unlike broad basic roles like Owner/Editor), supporting the least-privilege principle.

questions.question: What does BigQuery's on-demand pricing model primarily charge for?
options: A. Number of tables created
B. Amount of data scanned per query
C. Number of users with access
D. CPU hours of the query engine
questions.explain: On-demand BigQuery pricing bills per TB of data scanned by each query, which is why partitioning and clustering tables matters for cost.

questions.question: Which GCP service is the managed, horizontally-scalable NoSQL database with strong consistency, often used for mobile/web app backends?
options: A. Cloud SQL
B. Firestore
C. BigQuery
D. Memorystore
questions.explain: Firestore is a managed NoSQL document database with real-time sync and strong consistency, commonly used for mobile and web backends.

questions.question: What is the function of a GCP VPC Service Control perimeter?
options: A. It load-balances traffic across regions
B. It restricts data exfiltration by creating a security boundary around GCP resources/APIs
C. It encrypts data at rest automatically
D. It auto-scales Compute Engine instances
questions.explain: VPC Service Controls create a perimeter around GCP services to prevent data from being copied or accessed outside authorized networks, mitigating exfiltration.

questions.question: Which GKE node pool mode offloads node provisioning and management entirely to Google?
options: A. Standard mode
B. Autopilot mode
C. Preemptible mode
D. Zonal mode
questions.explain: GKE Autopilot fully manages node provisioning, sizing, and upgrades — you only manage workloads, and billing is per-pod resource request.

questions.question: What does Google Cloud's sustained use discount automatically apply to?
options: A. Any workload regardless of runtime
B. Compute Engine instances run for a significant portion of the billing month, without needing upfront commitment
C. Only preemptible VMs
D. Cloud Storage egress traffic
questions.explain: Sustained use discounts automatically reduce Compute Engine costs the longer an instance runs in a billing month — no reservation or upfront payment required.

questions.question: Which gcloud CLI command would you use to view your currently active authenticated account and project configuration?
options: A. gcloud config list
B. gcloud projects list
C. gcloud auth application-default login
D. gcloud init --console-only
questions.explain: 'gcloud config list' shows the active configuration, including the authenticated account, default project, and region/zone settings.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between traditional push-based CI/CD and GitOps?
options: A. GitOps doesn't use Git at all
B. In GitOps, an in-cluster agent pulls and reconciles the desired state from Git, instead of an external CI system pushing changes into the cluster
C. Push-based CD is always faster than GitOps
D. There is no real difference, just different marketing
questions.explain: GitOps flips the model: instead of CI holding cluster credentials and pushing changes, an in-cluster agent (like ArgoCD/Flux) pulls the desired state from Git and continuously reconciles the cluster to match it.

questions.question: In ArgoCD, what does setting both `prune: true` and `selfHeal: true` in syncPolicy.automated achieve?
options: A. It disables automatic syncing entirely
B. Resources removed from Git are deleted from the cluster, AND any manual cluster changes are automatically reverted to match Git
C. It only affects Helm-based applications
D. It encrypts secrets automatically
questions.explain: prune deletes cluster resources no longer declared in Git; selfHeal reverts any manual/out-of-band cluster change back to the Git-declared state — together they make Git the sole source of truth.

questions.question: What is the ArgoCD 'App-of-Apps' pattern used for?
options: A. Running ArgoCD inside another ArgoCD instance
B. Managing many Application CRDs through a single parent Application that points at a folder of child Application manifests
C. A way to disable GitOps for a specific namespace
D. A naming convention with no functional effect
questions.explain: App-of-Apps lets a single root Application sync an entire folder of other Application definitions, so you can manage dozens of microservice deployments by syncing one parent resource.

questions.question: Why should secret values generally NOT be committed directly to a GitOps repository, even in encrypted form with something like SOPS?
options: A. SOPS encryption is always broken and insecure

B. Git history is permanent — even if rotated, an old encrypted secret and its historical access remain auditable risk; many teams prefer External Secrets Operator so the value never touches Git at all
C. Kubernetes cannot read encrypted YAML
D. It is technically impossible to encrypt YAML files
questions.explain: SOPS and Sealed Secrets are legitimate options, but since Git history is immutable and widely accessible, many teams prefer External Secrets Operator — which pulls secrets from a vault at runtime so no secret material, encrypted or not, is ever stored in Git.

questions.question: What does it mean when an ArgoCD Application shows status 'OutOfSync'?
options: A. The application has crashed
B. The live cluster state differs from what's declared in Git
C. ArgoCD itself is down
D. The Git repository is unreachable
questions.explain: OutOfSync means ArgoCD's diff between the live cluster resources and the Git-declared manifests found a mismatch — the trigger for either an automated or manual sync.

questions.question: In Flux, what is the role of a Kustomization resource?
options: A. It defines a Docker image build
B. It applies a specific path from a watched GitRepository to the cluster, with pruning and health-check support
C. It only manages Helm charts, never raw YAML
D. It replaces the need for a GitRepository resource entirely
questions.explain: A Flux Kustomization points at a path within a GitRepository source and applies those manifests to the cluster, optionally pruning removed resources and waiting for health checks.

questions.question: What is the main practical difference between ArgoCD and Flux as GitOps tools?
options: A. Flux cannot deploy Kubernetes applications
B. ArgoCD ships a rich built-in web UI and is application-centric; Flux is a more composable toolkit of controllers with built-in image automation but no default UI
C. ArgoCD doesn't support Helm
D. They are functionally identical with no differences
questions.explain: Both are CNCF-graduated and implement the same GitOps principles, but ArgoCD centers on an Application CRD with a built-in UI, while Flux is a composable set of controllers (GitRepository/Kustomization/HelmRelease) with built-in image update automation.

questions.question: What is 'progressive delivery' in the context of GitOps tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger?
options: A. Deploying to all users simultaneously as fast as possible
B. Gradually shifting traffic to a new version (e.g. 5% → 25% → 100%) while monitoring metrics, with automatic rollback if thresholds are breached
C. A method for encrypting rollout manifests
D. Manually approving every single pod restart
questions.explain: Progressive delivery tools incrementally shift traffic to a new version while watching metrics like error rate and latency, automatically rolling back if the canary looks unhealthy — reducing blast radius versus an all-at-once deploy.

questions.question: What is the key operational difference between blue-green and canary deployments?
options: A. They are two names for the exact same deployment strategy
B. Canary shifts a percentage of traffic gradually to the new version; blue-green keeps two full environments and cuts over 100% of traffic at once, with instant rollback by flipping back
C. Blue-green only works with serverless functions, canary only with containers
D. Canary requires twice the infrastructure, blue-green requires none
questions.explain: Canary gradually increases traffic to the new version (e.g. 10% then 50% then 100%), while blue-green keeps both full environments running and switches all traffic at once — simpler to reason about and instantly reversible, at the cost of running double the infrastructure during the switch.

questions.question: What does a drift detection tool like driftctl actually check for?
options: A. Whether Terraform code passes a linter
B. Whether the LIVE infrastructure still matches what's declared in Terraform state — catching manual console changes Terraform doesn't know about
C. Network latency drift between AWS regions
D. Whether Docker images have drifted from their base image
questions.explain: Drift detection compares actual live infrastructure against the Terraform state file, flagging anything that changed outside of Terraform (like a manual console edit) — catching configuration decay that IaC scanning alone (which only checks code before deploy) would miss.

questions.question: What's the difference between Checkov (IaC scanning) and InSpec (compliance as code) in a DevSecOps pipeline?
options: A. They do the exact same thing and are interchangeable

B. Checkov scans your Terraform/Kubernetes CODE before deployment for misconfigurations; InSpec checks your LIVE, already-running infrastructure against compliance controls (e.g. CIS benchmarks) continuously
C. InSpec only works on AWS, Checkov only works on Azure
D. Checkov is a runtime security tool, InSpec is a static analysis tool
questions.explain: Checkov is a pre-deploy, shift-left check against your IaC source code; InSpec/compliance-as-code tools validate the actual running environment against compliance requirements on an ongoing basis — they're complementary, not redundant.

questions.question: In a GitHub Actions DAST job using OWASP ZAP, why would you run a 'baseline' scan before a 'full' active scan?
options: A. Baseline scans are passive (safe for any environment including prod); full/active scans send real attack payloads and should only run against staging/test, never production
B. There's no functional difference, it's just a naming convention
C. Baseline scans take longer to run than full scans
D. Full scans can only run locally, never in CI
questions.explain: ZAP's baseline scan is passive — it observes traffic without attacking — making it safe to run anywhere including production. A full/active scan actively sends attack payloads to find vulnerabilities, so it should only target non-production environments.
